topic: Types and Causes of Inflation in Economics
description: Inflation refers to the sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services over time, leading to a decrease in the purchasing power of money. It is a highly critical topic in macroeconomics.

sections.title: Basic Concepts of Inflation
sections.description: Fundamental definitions of inflation and other related macroeconomic conditions.

key_concepts.explanation: A macroeconomic situation where there is a sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services, and a consequent fall in the purchasing value of money.
The exact opposite of inflation, characterized by a sustained and continuous fall in the general price level. It is also known as negative inflation.
A decrease in the rate of inflation. Prices are still rising, but at a slower pace than before (e.g., the inflation rate dropping from 6% to 4%).
A paradoxical economic situation where high inflation, high unemployment, and stagnant economic growth coexist simultaneously.

sections.title: Main Causes of Inflation
sections.description: Analysis of the primary economic factors and drivers that cause prices to rise in an economy.

key_concepts.explanation: Occurs when aggregate demand in an economy outpaces aggregate supply. It is famously described as 'too much money chasing too few goods'.
Occurs when overall prices increase due to a rise in the cost of production factors, such as raw materials, energy, or wages.
Arises due to structural bottlenecks in the economy, such as poor infrastructure, supply chain disruptions, hoarding, and severe fluctuations in agricultural output.

sections.title: Types of Inflation based on Rates
sections.description: Classification of inflation based on the speed and intensity at which prices are rising.

key_concepts.explanation: When prices rise at a very slow and predictable rate, usually less than 3% annually. It is generally considered safe and essential for economic growth.
When the inflation rate is moderately high, roughly between 3% to 10% annually. It serves as a warning signal for the government and the Central Bank to control it.
When prices rise at double or triple-digit rates per year, such as 20%, 50%, or 100%. This causes severe economic instability and loss of confidence in the currency.
An unmanageable and extremely high rate of inflation where prices rise by 50% or more per month (e.g., historical crises in Zimbabwe and Venezuela). The currency completely loses its value.

sections.title: Measurement of Inflation and Indian Scenario
sections.description: Major indices used to measure inflation and the primary policies adopted in India.

key_concepts.explanation: Measures the changes in the prices of goods sold and traded in bulk by wholesale businesses to other businesses. Importantly, WPI does not include services.
Measures price changes from the perspective of a retail buyer. It includes both goods and services and reflects the true cost of living.
Calculated by removing highly volatile components, such as food and energy prices, from the headline inflation index to determine the underlying long-term inflation trend.

important_facts.fact: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) currently uses the Consumer Price Index (CPI-Combined) as the key metric for framing its Monetary Policy.
Based on the Urjit Patel Committee's recommendations, the legal inflation target in India is set at 4%, with a tolerance band of +/- 2% (i.e., maintaining it between 2% and 6%).

sections.title: Impact of Inflation and Related Principles
sections.description: The varying impact of inflation on different sections of society and a crucial econometric principle.

scientific_principles.application: Developed by A.W. Phillips, this curve illustrates that in the short run, inflation and unemployment have a stable and inverse relationship (higher inflation leads to lower unemployment, and vice versa).

key_associations.extra_info: Borrowers benefit during inflation because they repay their loans with money that has a lower purchasing power than when they initially borrowed it.
Lenders suffer a loss during inflation as the real value of the money returned to them decreases.
Their nominal income remains stagnant, but the cost of living rises rapidly, drastically reducing their purchasing power.
